query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Minor Mo addition will raise the high-temperature strength of equiatomic TiVNbTa without sacrificing its room-temperature ductility, making it a better W/CuCrZr interlayer.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc-melted, homogenised, single–phase BCC equiatomic TiVNbTa high-entropy alloy (≈800 MPa yield strength and ≈40 % tensile elongation at 300 K; ≈330 MPa yield strength in compression at 1273 K).
generation.intervention: Substitute 5 at.% of Ti with Mo to obtain Ti0.20V0.25Nb0.25Ta0.25Mo0.05 (hereafter ‘Ti-V-Nb-Ta-5Mo’), using identical melting and homogenisation schedules as the baseline alloy.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tests in Ar atmosphere at 300 K–1273 K, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹; no prior thermomechanical processing other than standard homogenisation (e.g. 1473 K, 24 h, water-quench).
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a single-phase BCC solid solution with increased average lattice distortion and suppressed high-temperature diffusion by Mo (sluggish diffusion effect).
generation.mechanism: Mo atoms (larger atomic size and high melting point) raise the lattice friction stress and decrease dislocation mobility (solid-solution strengthening) while delaying recovery and grain growth at elevated temperature; Mo’s high thermal conductivity (≈140 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹) also sustains heat flow across the W/interlayer/CuCrZr stack.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to TiVNbTa, Ti-V-Nb-Ta-5Mo will show ≈50 % higher 1273 K yield strength (≥500 MPa) and ≥30 % room-temperature tensile elongation, with thermal conductivity unchanged or slightly increased (±20 %).
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa: 330 MPa yield and 423 MPa compressive strength at 1273 K; ≈800 MPa yield and ≈40 % tensile strain at 300 K.
generation.boundary: Prediction expected to hold for Mo additions ≤10 at.% and temperatures ≤1273 K; above ≈1400 K or with higher Mo, brittle intermetallic precipitation may negate benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of ductility retention and thermal-conductivity change are uncertain; unforeseen phase separation during prolonged high-temperature exposure could offset strength gains.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce TiVNbTa and Ti-V-Nb-Ta-5Mo ingots by identical vacuum arc melting (five re-melts), homogenise at 1473 K for 24 h, water-quench. Cut cylindrical specimens (φ3 mm × 6 mm). Perform uniaxial compression tests at 300 K and 1273 K (10⁻³ s⁻¹). Measure thermal conductivity at 300 K and 800 K by laser flash analysis. Characterise phases by XRD and STEM-EDS before and after a 24 h exposure at 1273 K.
measurements: 0.2 % offset yield strength at 300 K and 1273 K
Plastic strain at fracture at 300 K
Thermal conductivity at 300 K and 800 K
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following hold for Ti-V-Nb-Ta-5Mo: (i) 1273 K yield strength ≤400 MPa (≤20 % gain over baseline), or (ii) room-temperature tensile elongation <30 %, or (iii) thermal conductivity drops by >20 % relative to baseline, or (iv) post-exposure microstructure shows >5 vol.% secondary (non-BCC) phases.
